title: Tamsin and the Interior
premise: After her mother's funeral, Odile Coldharbour returns to the family house to catalog a lifetime of silence, moving through rooms like a tenant awaiting eviction. Behind a wardrobe she finds a box of undelivered letters—her mother's, addressed to Odile across thirty years, each one sealed and never sent. Reading them, Odile uncovers the family secret everyone arranged themselves around: her mother gave up a child, and the letters were written to that child, not to her. As relatives converge on the house to contest the will and bury the past, Odile must decide whether to deliver the letters at last—knowing it will shatter the found family she built from the wreckage. In the end, she chooses truth over inheritance, mails the letters, and walks out of the house an owner of nothing but her own voice.
about_author: Sebastian Ravensworth is the pen name of a former estate archivist who spent a decade cataloging the unopened correspondence of the dead. They write literary fiction about inheritance, silence, and the families we assemble from what remains.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Three days after the funeral, Odile sleeps in the guest room of her childhood house, unable to claim the master bedroom or even her old one. She catalogs rooms for the solicitor like inventory. Emotional beat: grief expressed as bureaucratic detachment—the tenant who never signed a lease.

chapters.title: Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Cataloging continues; aunts and cousins call with claims on furniture before the will is read. Odile notices her mother's wardrobe is the only room untouched by dust. Emotional beat: the eerie sense that the house is withholding something, and so did her mother.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Moving the wardrobe to repair a warped floorboard, Odile finds a cavity lined with cedar and a box: forty-one sealed letters, dated across three decades, all addressed in her mother's hand. None were ever posted. Emotional beat: vertigo—the discovery that silence had architecture.

chapters.title: The First Letter
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, interwoven with the letter's text. The earliest letter, written when Odile was an infant, begins 'To the one I could not keep.' Odile realizes the letters are not to her. Emotional beat: betrayal braided with fascination; she cannot stop reading.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Cross-referencing dates and a birth certificate hidden in the lining, Odile deduces her mother bore a son at nineteen and surrendered him. Her father knew. Everyone knew. Emotional beat: the ground tilting—her whole identity was a curated exhibit.

chapters.title: Aunt Verity Arrives
chapters.summary: Verity's POV. Mother's sister sweeps in 'to help,' immediately taking stock of valuables and Odile's fragility. Verity's internal calculus reveals she has always managed the family's silences for a fee of influence. Emotional beat: menace dressed as kindness.

chapters.title: What Verity Knows
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Over sherry, Odile tests Verity with a half-truth about the box. Verity's face does something small and terrible. That night someone searches Odile's room. Emotional beat: the hunt beginning—she is no longer invisible, and visibility is dangerous.

chapters.title: Letters 1989–1994
chapters.summary: Odile's POV with letter interludes. The middle letters trace the brother's possible life: a name, a town, a school scholarship the mother secretly funded. Emotional beat: tenderness growing toward a stranger, and guilt that this love feels stolen from her own childhood.

chapters.title: The Will
chapters.summary: Solicitor's office; Odile's POV. The will leaves everything to Odile—but with a condition buried in clause nine: the house must remain 'unopened' for five years. Verity contests immediately. Emotional beat: even from the grave, her mother is still arranging the family around a secret.

chapters.title: Cousin Marcus
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The estranged cousin arrives, broke and hungry for the house, and offers Odile an alliance against Verity. He suspects what's in the box—he once found a letter as a boy and was made to forget. Emotional beat: wary kinship; two damaged people recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Fire That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A small fire starts in the study where the box is hidden; extinguished quickly, but the timing is unmistakable. Odile moves the letters into a bank vault, keeping only one. Emotional beat: fear hardening into resolve—they can burn paper, not what she now knows.

chapters.title: Letters 2001–2010
chapters.summary: Odile's POV with letter interludes. The later letters grow darker: the mother traced the son to a city, watched him once outside a bookshop, couldn't cross the street. Emotional beat: heartbreak of cowardice—love that stopped at the curb, and Odile's fury at being raised by that same restraint.

chapters.title: Verity's Bargain
chapters.summary: Verity's POV. Verity offers Odile a deal: surrender the letters, and Verity drops the will contest, preserving the fiction that protected them all—including, she claims, Odile herself. Emotional beat: temptation; the offer is genuinely kind and genuinely corrupting.

chapters.title: The Found Family
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Flashback chapter: how Odile, after her father's death, assembled a chosen family—a landlady, a librarian, a Sunday dinner table—because the blood family offered only roles, not love. Emotional beat: naming what she actually stands to lose if the secret detonates.

chapters.title: Marcus Confesses
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus admits he told Verity about the box years ago and was paid to stay silent; his alliance was penance and self-interest both. Odile forgives him conditionally. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid in small betrayals, and the possibility of earning trust back.

chapters.title: Clause Nine
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile rereads the will and understands: 'unopened' was her mother's final attempt to keep the letters sealed forever—and the reason Verity needs the box destroyed before probate ends. Emotional beat: clarity; the deadline is real, and time is running out.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Odile's POV with the final letter in full. Written weeks before death, unsent: 'If you are reading these, I failed twice—once to keep you, once to find you.' It names the son: Daniel Wren, a city two hours away. Emotional beat: the mother finally speaking plainly from beyond the arrangement of silence.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Long Room
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. At the family gathering before probate closes, Odile reads the first letter aloud to Verity, Marcus, and the assembled relatives. Verity's defense collapses into confession: she arranged the adoption, took the money, kept the ledger. Emotional beat: climax—the whole family's architecture cracking open in one room.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In the aftermath, relatives scatter or reconcile in small, imperfect ways. Odile walks the empty house one last time, returning objects to rooms, releasing the tenant's obligations. Emotional beat: exhalation; grief finally allowed to be ordinary.

chapters.title: Two Hours Away
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile drives to the city, finds the bookshop from the letters still standing, and learns Daniel Wren is alive, a teacher, unaware of any of it. She sits with the box on her knees for an hour. Emotional beat: threshold terror—the difference between knowing the truth and delivering it.

chapters.title: Delivery
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile posts all forty-one letters, then waits outside the bookshop as Daniel receives the first one and reads it standing in the doorway. Their eyes meet; she doesn't approach. Not yet. Emotional beat: quiet climax of choice—truth given without demand.

chapters.title: Owner of Nothing
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, epilogue. A year later: the house sold, proceeds split with Daniel by her own design, a new Sunday table set for old friends and one new, cautious correspondent. Odile signs her own name to something at last. Emotional beat: resolution—found family rebuilt on delivered words instead of kept silence.
